1.patient_information_and_chief_complain.text: Female patient, 57 years old, from Xincheng District, Xi'an City, was admitted to the Department of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine inpatient ward on Day 0, with the chief complaint of "intermittent fever and cough for more than half a year, with hemoptysis for 1 month." The patient developed intermittent fever after vaccination in approximately 6 months before Day 0, with a maximum temperature of 38.2℃; the fever usually occurred at dawn, and the temperature returned to normal after drinking water or activity. There were no associated symptoms such as myalgia, retro-orbital pain, joint pain, rash, chills, or profuse sweating. Thereafter, intermittent fever persisted, with temperature fluctuating between 37.2℃-37.5℃, occasionally accompanied by mild dry mouth and irritative dry cough, without hemoptysis, dizziness, headache, afternoon fever, fatigue, or night sweats. By approximately 3 months before Day 0, the above symptoms were still recurrent, accompanied by cough and copious white sticky sputum that was difficult to expectorate, so she presented to a hospital in Xi'an, where pneumonia was considered, and she was given 10 days of intravenous anti-infective treatment. At discharge, repeat chest CT showed slight absorption of the right lower lobe exudative change compared with before, and after discharge she sequentially received oral moxifloxacin hydrochloride for 1 week for anti-infective treatment. On Day -41, the patient developed hemoptysis without obvious precipitating cause, about more than 10 mouthfuls/day, consisting of old dark red bloody sputum, and again presented to a hospital in Xi'an. Chest CT showed multiple faint patchy infiltrative opacities of varying sizes. She then came emergently to our hospital, where chest CT showed multiple subpleural exudative lesions in both lungs, with hemorrhage considered. After emergency hemostatic treatment, she was transferred to the thoracic surgery ICU. Electronic bronchoscopy showed fresh bleeding in the dorsal segment of the right lower lobe; no other obvious abnormalities were seen. She was given symptomatic hemostatic treatment. Pulmonary infection was considered, and she received moxifloxacin hydrochloride and sodium chloride injection for anti-infective treatment for 8 days, after which the amount of hemoptysis was slightly relieved, but there were still small amounts of blood streaking, so she was transferred to our department on Day -33. NGS of bronchoalveolar lavage fluid suggested Gram-positive cocci (staphylococcal infection) and Mycobacterium kumamotonense (suspected). After admission to our department, she was given norvancomycin hydrochloride + latamoxef for anti-infective treatment. Meanwhile, repeat bronchoscopy showed a large amount of old bloody sputum obstructing the lumen in the left lower lobe and white mucoid sputum obstructing the basal segment of the right lower lobe; after suction, the lumens were patent, and biopsy was performed in the dorsal segment of the right lower lobe. Biopsy results showed (dorsal segment of the right lower lobe) chronic inflammation of bronchial mucosa-lung tissue with exudation/fibrous tissue proliferation and histiocytic proliferation, with focally active proliferation of some alveolar epithelial cells. After anti-infective treatment, the patient's temperature normalized, and blood in the sputum decreased compared with before. In conjunction with the pathology biopsy results, secondary organizing pneumonia (SOP) was considered, and prednisone acetate tablets 20 mg orally once daily were given, together with azithromycin tablets 500 mg once daily. On Day -22, repeat chest CT showed slight absorption and improvement of the lesion in the dorsal segment of the right lower lobe compared with before. Total IgE was 159. After discharge, she continued oral corticosteroid and azithromycin treatment. Her cough and sputum symptoms improved, but she still had intermittent blood-streaked sputum, alternating between dark red and bright red. On Day -2, chest CT at outpatient follow-up showed, compared with the film from Day -22, that the bilateral pulmonary lesions had slightly increased in size and number, with hemorrhage considered. For further diagnosis and treatment, she was readmitted on Day 0. On the day of admission, the patient had more than 30 mouthfuls of hemoptysis, with dark red bloody sputum in the morning gradually changing to bright red bloody sputum, accompanied by shortness of breath, mainly during inspiration. Past history: the patient had allergic rhinitis for more than 5 years; denied allergy history; no other abnormalities were reported. Personal history: long-term resident of Xi'an; denied smoking, alcohol, and exposure to drugs or toxic substances. Family history: both parents deceased; mother had hemoptysis for many years, cause unknown; no other remarkable family history. Admission examination: T 36.6℃, P 107 beats/min, R 22 breaths/min, BP 108/56 mmHg, SpO2 92-95% (without oxygen). Lips slightly rosy. No rash over the whole body, no palpable superficial lymphadenopathy, no chest deformity, symmetric bilateral respiratory movement, no increased tactile fremitus, clear percussion note over both lungs, clear breath sounds in both lungs, a few moist rales heard in both lower lungs, no Velcro rales, and no pleural friction rub. No precordial bulge. Apical impulse located at the fifth intercostal space, 0.5 cm medial to the left midclavicular line. No palpable thrill. Cardiac borders not enlarged. Heart rate 108 beats/min, regular rhythm, no obvious increase or decrease in heart sounds, and no pathologic murmur heard in any valve auscultation area. Abdomen flat and soft, no hepatosplenomegaly, no abdominal tenderness or abdominal muscle guarding. No edema in both lower extremities.

differential_diagnoses.name: Diffuse alveolar hemorrhage syndrome (including pulmonary capillaritis-associated alveolar hemorrhage)
supporting_evidence: The chief complaint was "intermittent fever and cough for more than half a year, accompanied by hemoptysis for 1 month," and on the day of admission, "more than 30 episodes of hemoptysis, with dark red bloody sputum since morning gradually changing to bright red bloody sputum."

Multiple chest CT scans showed "multiple subpleural exudative-like lesions in both lungs, hemorrhage considered" and "bilateral lung lesions slightly enlarged and increased in number compared with before, hemorrhage considered"

Flexible bronchoscopy showed "fresh bleeding in the dorsal segment of the right lower lobe"; subsequent bronchoscopy again showed "old bloody sputum obstructing the lumens of both lower lobes," consistent with active/recurrent bleeding in the lower respiratory tract.
Associated with shortness of breath, SpO2 92-95% (not on oxygen), suggesting possible hemorrhage-related impairment of gas exchange
Hemoglobin 101 g/L, anemia is present; in conjunction with recurrent hemoptysis, this supports the possibility of blood loss/intra-alveolar hemorrhage
The attached pathology images show eosinophilic hemorrhagic material within the alveolar spaces and inflammatory changes in the alveolar septa, consistent with alveolar hemorrhagic lesions.
opposing_evidence: ANA panel (-), vasculitis panel (-), not supportive of alveolar hemorrhage caused by a typical connective tissue disease or ANCA-associated vasculitis
Phase I information did not provide evidence of renal involvement, rash, arthritis, or other findings of pulmonary-renal syndrome or systemic vasculitis.

differential_diagnoses.name: Organizing pneumonia (secondary or cryptogenic, with hemorrhagic manifestations)
supporting_evidence: The pathology results indicated "chronic inflammation of the bronchial mucosa and lung tissue with exudation/fibrous tissue hyperplasia and histiocytic proliferation, with active proliferation of some alveolar epithelial cells"

After prior corticosteroid treatment, the "cough and sputum production symptoms were relieved," and repeat chest CT on Day -22 showed that the "lesion in the dorsal segment of the right lower lobe was slightly absorbed/improved compared with before," supporting an inflammatory/organizing lesion component.
Chest CT shows multiple exudative lesions in both lungs, some located subpleurally, consistent with the multifocal peripheral distribution imaging features seen in organizing pneumonia
The attached pathology images show organizing fibrous tissue within the alveoli and a chronic inflammatory cell reaction, supporting organizing pneumonia-like changes.
opposing_evidence: Organizing pneumonia usually presents predominantly with cough, fever, and dyspnea; the patient's recurrent marked hemoptysis and even active bleeding are relatively prominent, which cannot be fully explained by organizing pneumonia alone.

During continued treatment with oral corticosteroids and azithromycin, follow-up CT suggested that the bilateral lung lesions were slightly enlarged and increased in number compared with before, with hemorrhage considered, indicating that organizing pneumonia alone was insufficient to explain the findings.

differential_diagnoses.name: Infectious pneumonia/hemorrhagic pulmonary infection (predominantly bacterial, including staphylococcal-associated infection)
supporting_evidence: Early in the course of illness, there was fever, cough, and cough with white sticky sputum; the patient was previously treated at another hospital for "pneumonia"
Bronchoscopic lavage fluid NGS indicated "G+ cocci (staphylococcal infection)"
After anti-infective treatment, “body temperature returned to normal, and blood in the sputum decreased compared with before,” suggesting that some symptoms responded to anti-infective therapy.
Chest CT shows multiple infiltrative lesions, which may overlap radiographically with infectious infiltrates.
A few moist rales were heard in both lower lungs, supporting the possibility of lower respiratory tract inflammation/exudation.
opposing_evidence: PCT 0.05 (-), not supportive of active severe bacterial infection
WBC 4.25×10^9/L, ESR 13 mm/h; the inflammatory response is not elevated

After multiple courses of anti-infective treatment, the patient continued to have recurrent hemoptysis and increasing imaging lesions, suggesting that simple bacterial pneumonia is an insufficient explanation.

differential_diagnoses.name: Pulmonary tuberculosis or nontuberculous mycobacterial lung disease
supporting_evidence: The course of illness has been prolonged for more than half a year, with recurrent fever, cough, and hemoptysis, consistent with the clinical course seen in chronic mycobacterial infection.
BALF NGS suggested "Mycobacterium chelonae (suspected)"
Chest CT indicates multiple lesions in both lungs, and the condition was not completely controlled after conventional antibacterial therapy; mycobacterial infection should be considered.
The patient has persistent blood-streaked sputum; hemoptysis is one of the common manifestations of TB/nontuberculous mycobacterial infection.
opposing_evidence: The first-phase text explicitly states: “no afternoon low-grade fever, fatigue, or night sweats”
The attached CT images do not show characteristic findings more supportive of TB/NTM, such as typical cavitation or a tree-in-bud pattern.
In the first-stage information, mycobacteria were only described as "suspected," lacking definitive microbiological evidence.

differential_diagnoses.name: Pulmonary malignant neoplasm (e.g., mucinous adenocarcinoma/hemorrhagic tumor)
supporting_evidence: The patient is 57 years old and has a persistent cough that does not resolve, with recurrent hemoptysis; these are warning signs that warrant vigilance for a pulmonary tumor.

After anti-infective and corticosteroid treatment, the imaging lesions still showed slight enlargement and increase in number compared with before, suggesting that a neoplastic lesion cannot be completely excluded.
Bronchoscopy localized active bleeding to the posterior basal segment of the right lower lobe, with a focal bleeding source present
The pathology description states "focally active proliferation of alveolar epithelial cells"; although nonspecific, caution is needed in differentiating reactive hyperplasia from tumor.
opposing_evidence: Bronchoscopic biopsy results did not indicate a definite tumor, but were mainly characterized by chronic inflammation with exudation/fibrous tissue hyperplasia and histiocytic hyperplasia.
The attached CT images and text description did not show definite direct evidence of tumor, such as an occupying mass or hilar/mediastinal lymphadenopathy.
The patient has no history of smoking.

differential_diagnoses.name: Hemoptysis caused by bronchial/pulmonary vascular malformation or other focal vascular lesions
supporting_evidence: The patient has recurrent significant hemoptysis, and bronchoscopy indicated "fresh bleeding was visible in the dorsal segment of the right lower lobe," suggesting a possible focal bleeding source.
On the day of admission, bright red bloody sputum increased and was accompanied by shortness of breath, consistent with active airway bleeding.
The patient's mother had a history of hemoptysis for many years, of unknown cause, suggesting that certain familial bleeding tendencies or vascular abnormalities cannot be completely excluded.
opposing_evidence: No definite direct imaging evidence of a vascular mass or arteriovenous malformation was seen on the chest CT report text or the accompanying images.
Pathology is more suggestive of inflammatory/organizing changes, with no evidence provided for vascular malformation.

There was no rash on the skin of the entire body, and the information from the first phase also did not describe epistaxis, mucosal telangiectasia, or other manifestations supporting hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia.

recommended_exams.exam: Anti-glomerular basement membrane antibody and other nephritis-related antibody panel

stage2_input.text: Further examination results after admission: urinalysis and stool routine + OB were normal. Coagulation studies, cardiac enzymes, BNP, fasting blood glucose, and thyroid function were normal. Infectious disease panel: hepatitis B five-panel, hepatitis C, HIV, and syphilis (-). Fungal tests: GM test and G test (-). Comprehensive viral panel: cytomegalovirus antibody IgG (CMV-IgG), herpes simplex virus type I antibody (HSV) IgG positive, rubella virus antibody IgG (-), Epstein-Barr virus antibody (-). Nine-item respiratory pathogen panel, Mycoplasma and Chlamydia antibodies were all negative (-). TB: Mycobacterium tuberculosis antibody negative; PPD skin test (1:2000 +, 1:10000 -); interferon-gamma release assay (-). Tumor markers: all five lung tumor markers were normal. Comprehensive immunoglobulin panel negative. Anti-glomerular basement membrane antibody negative. ANA, ANCA, vasculitis panel (3 items), rheumatoid factor, anti-CCP, complement C3, complement C4, autoimmune liver panel, and antiphospholipid antibodies were negative. Myositis and scleroderma antibodies were negative. Allergen testing negative. Sputum examination: hemosiderin-laden cells positive (sputum). Cardiac + bilateral lower extremity venous Doppler ultrasound: no obvious abnormality of intracardiac structure; measured left ventricular systolic function within the normal range. Segmental blood flow in the deep veins of both lower extremities was patent. Echocardiography: mild tricuspid regurgitation, pericardial effusion, measured left ventricular systolic function within the normal range. Pulmonary function testing: mild obstructive ventilatory dysfunction; mildly impaired pulmonary ventilatory function, normal diffusing capacity; bronchodilator test negative. FeNO test: 7 ppb. Fiberoptic bronchoscopy: a large amount of fresh blood was seen in the trachea, the bronchi of both upper lobes, and the right lower lobe bronchus; a small amount of pigment spot deposition was seen in the segmental bronchus of the left upper lobe; the bronchial lumens at all levels of the left lower lobe and right middle lobe were patent, the mucosa was smooth, and no neoplasm was seen under bronchoscopy. Because a large amount of fresh blood was seen in the trachea, biopsy was not performed to prevent worsening bleeding; only a protected brush specimen was obtained from the anterior segment of the right upper lobe and sent for pathology. Pathologic cytology: no tumor cells identified. Labial gland biopsy pathology: (lower lip labial gland) scattered lymphocyte and plasma cell infiltration between the submitted labial salivary glands. CBC with 5-part differential: no obvious abnormality. Rheumatology panel (serum): rheumatoid factor 18.30 IU/mL1. ECG showed: 1. Sinus rhythm; 2. Essentially normal ECG.

recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient has had recurrent fever and cough for more than half a year, followed by persistent hemoptysis progressing to bright red bloody sputum. Repeated chest CT suggested multiple bilateral pulmonary exudative lesions and raised concern for hemorrhage. The condition had previously fluctuated after anti-infective and corticosteroid treatment, suggesting that infection alone or inflammation alone cannot fully explain the presentation. Bronchoscopy has shown fresh blood at multiple sites in both lungs, suggesting that the lesion is located at the lower respiratory tract/alveolar level. Pathogen testing of bronchoalveolar lavage fluid can directly assess whether there is local evidence of bacteria, fungi, mycobacteria, or other infection, thereby addressing the key question of whether the alveolar hemorrhage was triggered by infection or accompanied by infection. At the same time, before subsequently considering immunosuppressive treatment such as corticosteroid pulse therapy, active infection needs to be excluded as much as possible in order to reduce treatment risk and guide whether to continue, adjust, or stop the anti-infective regimen.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Gram stain: Gram-positive cocci +, Gram-negative cocci -, Gram-positive bacilli -, Gram-negative bacilli +, no fungi detected
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: At disease onset, the patient had fever, cough, and expectoration of white sticky sputum. At an outside hospital, the patient was treated as having pneumonia, and previous BAL NGS suggested possible Staphylococcal infection. After anti-infective treatment, the body temperature and blood-streaked sputum partially improved; therefore, it is still necessary to rapidly determine whether a bacterial lower respiratory tract infection is present. Gram stain can rapidly provide direct clues such as G+ cocci or G- bacilli on BAL fluid specimens, helping to distinguish infectious exudation from noninfectious lesions predominantly characterized by alveolar hemorrhage, and can provide a basis for empiric antimicrobial selection. In particular, in this case, it is necessary to determine whether active bacterial infection is present before continuing evaluation of the cause of diffuse alveolar hemorrhage and preparing to intensify glucocorticoid therapy, in order to avoid mistakenly treating infectious hemorrhage as an immune-mediated disease.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Acid-fast stain: no acid-fast bacilli seen
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient's course has been prolonged for more than half a year, with recurrent hemoptysis, multiple lesions in both lungs, and poor control with conventional anti-infective therapy. Previous NGS of lavage fluid also suggested possible Mycobacterium terrae; therefore, TB or nontuberculous mycobacterial pulmonary disease has remained an important differential diagnosis. Although acid-fast staining has limited sensitivity, it can provide rapid initial screening for active mycobacterial infection and address the key question of whether the recurrent hemoptysis and pulmonary opacities are caused by mycobacterial infection. If acid-fast staining is positive, it will directly affect isolation requirements, antimycobacterial treatment decisions, and the safety of glucocorticoid use; even if negative, in combination with subsequent species identification and nucleic acid testing, it can also help progressively exclude infectious etiologies and support the related diagnoses of diffuse alveolar hemorrhage syndrome and hemosiderosis.

The patient’s imaging showed multiple bilateral pulmonary infiltrative lesions. The patient had previously received multiple courses of anti-infective therapy and corticosteroid treatment, raising clinical concern for opportunistic infection, especially invasive fungal infection. Although the main manifestations were recurrent hemoptysis and alveolar hemorrhage, fungal infection can also cause pulmonary infiltrates, hemoptysis, and even hemorrhagic lesions. The G test is used to screen for fungal cell wall components associated with invasive fungal infection and can help determine whether a deep fungal infection is present, thereby addressing the question of whether the current pulmonary lesions are complicated by or caused by fungal infection. The result of this test is of important value in determining whether high-dose corticosteroid pulse therapy can be administered with relative safety and whether additional antifungal therapy is needed.

In this patient, the disease course has been prolonged, the pulmonary lesions have shown recurrent changes, and glucocorticoid therapy has been administered; vigilance is required for pulmonary hemorrhage caused by invasive fungal infection such as Aspergillus or coexisting with the primary disease. The GM test has high suggestive value for invasive Aspergillus infection and can complement the G test to further evaluate fungal etiologies. The clinical purpose of performing this test is to exclude fungal infection such as Aspergillus as much as possible in the differential diagnosis of alveolar hemorrhage, and to avoid rash intensification of immunosuppressive therapy when infection has not been clarified; at the same time, if positive, it may significantly alter the subsequent treatment pathway, add antifungal therapy, and reassess the glucocorticoid regimen.

The patient has long-term fever, cough, recurrent hemoptysis, and multiple pulmonary lesions that have persisted without resolution. Previous evidence suggestive of mycobacteria has not been completely excluded, and a single negative acid-fast stain, TB antibody, and IGRA is insufficient to completely rule out TB or nontuberculous mycobacterial infection. The purpose of Mycobacterium tuberculosis species identification is to further determine whether this is Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex or other mycobacteria, thereby addressing the central diagnostic question of whether the chronic pulmonary lesions and hemoptysis are caused by mycobacterial infection. This result is critical for confirming the diagnosis, excluding alternative diagnoses, determining whether anti-TB/anti-NTM therapy is needed, and assessing infection risk before steroid pulse therapy.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Respiratory pathogen nucleic acid tests were all negative
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient had recurrent fever, cough, and sputum production, which then progressed to hemoptysis. Imaging showed multiple bilateral pulmonary infiltrates. Common bacterial infection, atypical pathogen infection, and noninfectious alveolar hemorrhage can overlap clinically and on imaging. Respiratory pathogen nucleic acid testing can rapidly cover a variety of common pathogens and help improve the efficiency of etiologic evaluation, especially in the setting of potentially reduced culture positivity after multiple prior courses of anti-infective therapy. This test is primarily intended to address whether viruses, Mycoplasma, Chlamydia, or other respiratory pathogens are still involved in the current illness; if the result is negative, then together with negative G/GM and negative acid-fast staining, it further supports the diagnosis of noninfectious alveolar hemorrhage and provides a safety basis for a subsequent glucocorticoid-based treatment strategy.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Bone marrow biopsy pathology: Features: 1. Hypercellular bone marrow with decreased adipose tissue; 2. Markedly active granulocytic proliferation, with all maturation stages present; eosinophils are seen; 3. Decreased erythroid proliferation, scattered cells are seen; 4. Megakaryocytes are not decreased. Impression: Markedly active granulocytic proliferation; please correlate with the clinical history.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient has recurrent hemoptysis, imaging manifestations of alveolar hemorrhage, and evidence of anemia. Although coagulation function and the peripheral blood routine showed no obvious abnormalities, in the differential diagnosis of diffuse alveolar hemorrhage it is still necessary to exclude hematologic diseases, myeloproliferative abnormalities, or other diseases that may cause a bleeding tendency, anemia, and abnormal inflammatory responses. Bone marrow biopsy pathology can assess the state of bone marrow proliferation, the proportions of the various cell lineages, and whether infiltration, abnormal proliferation, or other underlying hematologic diseases are present at the level of tissue architecture, thereby addressing the question of whether a hematologic disease is involved in or explains the recurrent bleeding and anemia. This examination is valuable for excluding important differential diagnoses, assessing the risk of subsequent glucocorticoid therapy, and clarifying the nature of the anemia/bone marrow reactive changes.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Bone marrow cytology: bone marrow findings with markedly active granulocytic hyperplasia.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: In the setting of recurrent alveolar hemorrhage, a protracted disease course, and an unclear etiology, normal peripheral blood and coagulation studies alone are still insufficient to completely exclude hematologic disease. Bone marrow cytology can more directly assess morphologic changes in cells of each lineage, determine the proliferative status of the granulocytic, erythroid, and megakaryocytic lineages, and identify whether abnormal cells are present; it is complementary to the pathology of bone marrow biopsy. Clinically, this examination is performed to determine whether the anemia is consistent with reactive changes after blood loss and whether there is an underlying bone marrow disorder or hematologic disease causing a bleeding tendency, thereby further excluding hematologic differential diagnoses and providing a more comprehensive safety assessment for subsequent treatment.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Hemosiderin-laden macrophages identified in BALF and sputum: positive
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient’s core manifestations are recurrent hemoptysis, shortness of breath, and diffuse faint infiltrative opacities in both lungs. Bronchoscopy shows fresh blood at multiple sites. Diffuse alveolar hemorrhage is highly suspected clinically, but more direct evidence is needed to prove that the bleeding is located within the alveoli rather than only within the airways. Examination of BALF for hemosiderin-laden macrophages is an important test for confirming recurrent intra-alveolar bleeding, because alveolar macrophages form hemosiderin after phagocytosing red blood cells, which can reflect prior and ongoing alveolar hemorrhage. This test mainly addresses the key question of whether this truly constitutes an alveolar hemorrhage syndrome, and, together with results such as negative infectious pathogen studies and negative autoantibodies, can support the diagnosis of pulmonary hemosiderosis, while also helping explain the imaging infiltrative opacities and anemia and guiding the subsequent treatment direction centered on glucocorticoids.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Hemosiderin-laden macrophages identified in BALF and sputum: positive
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient has recurrent blood-streaked sputum and hemoptysis, with active changes in the condition, requiring simple and repeatable evidence to support alveolar hemorrhage. Although testing sputum for hemosiderin-laden macrophages is less direct than BALF, it is a less invasive examination that can be repeated dynamically and can provide important clues when the patient's hemoptysis persists or repeated bronchoscopy is not advisable. The clinical significance of this test is to further demonstrate that the bleeding does not originate solely from the large airways, but is related to recurrent intra-alveolar hemorrhage; when the sputum result is consistently positive with BALF, it can significantly increase diagnostic confidence for alveolar hemorrhage syndrome and pulmonary hemosiderosis, and help exclude simple infectious blood-streaked sputum or focal bronchial bleeding, providing a basis for evaluation of glucocorticoid treatment efficacy and follow-up of the condition.

7.key_confirmatory_exam_information.text: Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid results: Day +22, [Etiology] Gram stain: G+ cocci+, G- cocci-, G+ bacilli-, G- bacilli+; no fungi detected. Acid-fast stain: no acid-fast bacilli seen. G and GM tests were negative; Mycobacterium tuberculosis species identification and respiratory pathogen nucleic acid testing were both negative. Bone marrow biopsy pathology: Description: 1. Bone marrow hyperplasia was active, with decreased adipose tissue; 2. Granulocytic hyperplasia was markedly active, with all stages seen; eosinophils were present; 3. Erythroid hyperplasia was decreased, scattered cells were seen; 4. Megakaryocytes were not decreased. Impression: Granulocytic hyperplasia was markedly active; please correlate with the medical history. Bone marrow cytology: bone marrow picture with markedly active granulocytic hyperplasia. BALF and sputum were positive for hemosiderin-laden macrophages, therefore an in-hospital multidisciplinary consultation was requested.

images.near_text: Follow-up chest CT (see Figure 8) showed partial absorption and improvement of the lesions compared with the previous study.

diagnostic_basis: 1. The patient is a middle-aged or elderly woman
2. Recurrent blood-streaked sputum, diffuse faint infiltrative opacities in both lungs, dyspnea, hemosiderin-laden cells positive in sputum
3. Autoantibodies, ESR, vasculitis antibodies, rheumatologic panel, anti-glomerular basement membrane antibody, etc. were all negative
4. After corticosteroid pulse therapy, the patient's symptoms improved, and imaging findings showed interval resolution.

treatment_plan: Methylprednisolone 240 mg per dose, once daily, was given as pulse therapy for 5 consecutive days.
Subsequently, prednisone acetate tablets were given sequentially at 1 mg/kg/d; the patient weighed 50 kg and was given 50 mg orally once daily.
treatment_response: The patient's hemoptysis improved markedly, and repeat chest CT showed marked absorption compared with that at admission.

After 2 weeks of treatment with oral prednisone acetate 50 mg once daily, the patient returned for follow-up. The patient stated that since discharge there had been no further blood-streaked sputum, and no cough, sputum production, or shortness of breath. Body temperature was normal.
Repeat chest CT showed partial absorption and improvement of the lesions compared with the previous study, and the remaining lesions were stable
